897.title: The flute the gopis could only hear
897.hook: the gopis can only hear Krishna's flute from the village, and the whole forest stops to listen
897.carry: hearing about God is already bhakti
897.tomorrow: why would the gopis be jealous of a piece of bamboo?
897.howItsDone: Hindus gather to hear the Bhagavata told aloud in katha, often over seven days (a Bhagavata saptah), and to sing God's names in kirtan; the chapter on the flute is read and sung in devotion, and temple images show Krishna holding his flute.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-NINETY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Govardhan lifted. The storm came down on the village, and Krishna, Giridhari, held up a hill so everyone who ran to him could shelter underneath.
screen: `GOVARDHAN LIFTED.` · `GIRIDHARI SHELTERS EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: A calf is drinking from its mother, and it stops. The milk is still in its mouth. It doesn't swallow. It just stands there, ears up. Somewhere past the pasture, among the trees, someone is playing a flute. That calf comes from the Bhagavata Purana, from a chapter where the women of Vraja, the gopis, stay behind in the village while Krishna takes the cows to the forest. They can't see him. They can only hear him. So they tell each other what the sound is doing to everything it reaches.
screen: `A CALF FORGETS TO SWALLOW.` → `A FLUTE IN THE TREES.` → `THE GOPIS CAN ONLY HEAR.`

segments.voice: In this chapter Krishna doesn't teach anyone. He just plays, walking into the autumn forest with his brother Balarama and the herd. The gopis fill in the picture from memory: a peacock feather in his hair, a yellow cloth, a garland of forest flowers, his lips on the bamboo. Then they turn to the listeners. The cows lift their ears and drink in the sound; the calves stand with milk in their mouths. The birds settle on the branches and close their eyes. The rivers, the gopis say, slow their current and reach out with their waves to hold his feet. Even the clouds drift over him to give him shade. Not priests, not kings: cows, birds, water, weather. And the gopis themselves? At home, at their work. They can't see him. They can only hear him, and tell each other about him, and that is enough to fill them. Hindus take this very seriously. Later in the same Bhagavata, the boy Prahlada names nine ways of bhakti, loving devotion to God, and the first two are hearing about him and singing about him. The gopis are doing both, from their kitchens. That's why Hindus gather for katha, where a teller reads and explains the Bhagavata for days, sometimes a whole week, and for kirtan, singing God's names together. Nobody in the room sees Krishna. They listen, like a calf that forgot to swallow.
screen: `HE WALKS INTO THE AUTUMN FOREST.` · `COWS, BIRDS, RIVERS, CLOUDS.` · `THE GOPIS HEAR, BUT CAN'T SEE.` · then, large: `HEARING IS THE FIRST BHAKTI.`

segments.voice: Be one of the listeners in the forest. Let your eyes close or soften, and let sounds come to you, the room, the street, your own breath, without naming them. If a sound pulls you into thinking, come back with the next one. If you pray, softly hum one of Krishna's names, Gopala or Govinda, and listen to it as if it were the flute calling. If you don't, let one sound stand for something you love, and just listen.
The flute. Krishna's bamboo flute, whose music, the gopis say, stops cows, birds, deer, rivers and clouds in the forest of Vraja.

898.title: Why the gopis envied a flute
898.hook: a gopi is jealous of a piece of bamboo, and the hollow reed turns out to be the lesson
898.carry: empty of ego, like krishna's flute
898.tomorrow: who answers when the flute calls at night?
898.howItsDone: Devotees sing and recite the gopis' words about the flute from the Bhagavata, honor Krishna as Murlidhar, the one who holds the flute, and many close an action with Krishnarpanam astu, offering it to him.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-NINETY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the flute. The gopis could only hear it from the village, and hearing about Krishna was already their devotion.
screen: `THE FLUTE.` · `HEARING IS ALREADY BHAKTI.`

segments.voice: What did a stick do to deserve this? That's the gopis' question, and they're not joking. They're still in the village, still listening, and one of them says what the others are thinking. Krishna's lips are on that flute all day. It's a length of bamboo cut from some riverbank, with no voice of its own, no family, no story. And it gets closer to him than any of them. So they ask, half in envy and half in wonder: what good thing did this flute ever do?
screen: `WHAT DID A STICK DO?` → `CLOSER TO HIM THAN ANY OF THEM.` → `FROM THE SIDE OF THE FLUTE.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata gives the question to one gopi. What good did this flute ever do, she asks, that it enjoys the sweetness of his lips, a sweetness the gopis feel is theirs, and leaves them only what's left over? Then she answers herself, in a strange and lovely way. She looks at the bamboo's family. The lakes and rivers whose water raised it are glad: their lotuses open like hair standing up on skin. And the trees, the bamboo's elders, let their sap run down like tears, the way old people weep with joy when someone in the family turns out devoted. So halfway through her sentence, envy turns into praise. Now look at what a flute is. A hollow reed. Breath goes in one end and comes out as music; the flute adds nothing but the empty space. This is one of the best-loved readings in Krishna devotion: the flute is close to him because there's nothing inside it in the way. A reed packed full makes no sound. So the devotee's prayer is to be hollowed out, emptied of ahankara, the ego that keeps saying me and mine, so that Krishna's breath makes the music. Devotees call him Murlidhar, the one who holds the flute. That's a reading teachers give, not a line in the chapter. The chapter just leaves us with a woman in a village, jealous of a piece of bamboo, and then glad for it.
screen: `WHAT GOOD DID THIS FLUTE EVER DO?` · `THE RIVERS AND TREES ARE PROUD.` · `A HOLLOW REED, NOTHING IN THE WAY.` · then, large: `EMPTY OF EGO, FULL OF HIS MUSIC.`

segments.voice: Many Krishna devotees close a task or a meal with two words: Krishnarpanam astu, let this be an offering to Krishna. It hands the credit back, the way a flute hands back the breath. Breathe like a reed now: in without grabbing, out without pushing. With each exhale, let go of one small need to be right, or noticed, or first. Then pick one thing you will do today and offer it ahead of time. If you pray, say the words. If you don't, just picture doing it with nothing of yours in the way.

899.title: The milk left on the fire
899.hook: on the autumn full moon the flute calls, and the gopis go just as they are
899.carry: bhakti comes as it is, like the gopis
899.tomorrow: a king stops the story: how could this love be holy?
899.howItsDone: The opening of the rasa lila chapters, with the gopis leaving their work at the sound of the flute, is recited at katha and sung by Krishna devotees, and teachers of bhakti point to the gopis as devotion's model.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-NINETY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the flute again, a gopi jealous of a hollow reed, and the reading that it is close to Krishna because nothing inside is in the way.
screen: `THE FLUTE.` · `EMPTY OF EGO, LIKE HIS FLUTE.`

segments.voice: The milk is on the fire. Someone is halfway through milking a cow. Someone is serving food to her family. Someone has a baby at her breast. It's an autumn night in Vraja, the moon full and coming up red over the trees, and every house is in the middle of something. Then, from the forest, the flute. Not the daytime music the gopis talked about from a distance. This time, the Bhagavata says, the sound is calling them.
screen: `THE MILK IS ON THE FIRE.` → `A FULL MOON OVER THE TREES.` → `THIS TIME, THE FLUTE CALLS.`

segments.voice: The text slows down and goes house by house. The women hear the flute and go, each one exactly as she is. The one milking leaves the cow. The one boiling milk leaves the pot on the fire. The one cooking leaves the food unserved. The one feeding a child, the one eating her own dinner: all of them stand up and go. Some were dressing, and they go with their ornaments in disarray. Husbands, fathers and brothers try to stop them; they don't turn around. And some, the Bhagavata adds, were kept inside, and those women shut their eyes and went to him in meditation instead. Why linger on the half-finished jobs? Because the list is the point. Nobody finishes anything or makes herself presentable first. And notice who these are: not sages, not priests, not scholars of the Veda. Cowherd women with milk on the stove. Yet Hindu tradition holds them up as the very picture of bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras, a short classic on devotion, points to the gopis of Vraja as its example. Devotional readers hear the soul answering God here. It doesn't arrive polished or qualified. It comes as it is, and even the ones who can't leave the house reach him by remembering. The Bhagavata doesn't let the scene pass unexamined, though. Right after this, the king who's listening stops the story with a hard question. That's tomorrow.
screen: `EACH ONE GOES EXACTLY AS SHE IS.` · `SOME KEPT INSIDE GO IN MEDITATION.` · `NOT SAGES. COWHERD WOMEN.` · then, large: `THE GOPIS: BHAKTI'S EXAMPLE.`

segments.voice: Notice what you just set down to be here, a phone, a cup, a list, and leave it untidied. Then do what the women kept inside did: close your eyes and turn toward him. If you pray, say one name, Krishna, Govinda, or the name of God you use, silently with each breath, and come just as you are, without fixing anything first. When the half-done things tug, notice the tug and come back to the name. If you don't pray, rest your attention on someone you love, as you are, unfinished.
The flute. On the autumn night, the sound that calls the gopis out of their houses, mid-task, just as they are.

900.howItsDone: The rasa lila chapters of the Bhagavata are recited at katha and sung by Krishna devotees, and danced in the Ras Lila performances of Vrindavan; many temples keep the autumn full moon, Sharad Purnima, as the night of the rasa, and teachers in the devotional traditions present it as a picture of the soul's love for God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the flute on the full-moon night. The gopis left the milk on the fire and went just as they were, the tradition's own picture of bhakti.
screen: `THE FLUTE.` · `BHAKTI COMES AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: Before the dance, a king interrupts. In the Bhagavata, the sage Shuka is telling this story to King Parikshit, who has just heard about the women running into the forest at night. He stops the story. These women, he says, knew Krishna as a beloved, not as the highest truth. Their minds were full of him the way a lover's mind is full. How could that set them free? It's a fair question, and the text answers it before going one step further.
screen: `A KING INTERRUPTS.` → `THEY KNEW HIM AS A BELOVED.` → `HOW COULD THAT SET THEM FREE?`

segments.voice: Shuka's answer goes back to an earlier story: Shishupala, a king who hated Krishna, spent his life thinking of him in rage, and still reached him in the end. If hatred fixed on him could do that, Shuka says, then whoever turns the whole mind toward him, in desire or anger, fear, affection, kinship or friendship, becomes absorbed in him. What matters is where the mind is pointed. That's a big idea in Hindu bhakti: God isn't reached only through calm, correct feelings. Whatever you truly feel, turned wholly toward him, becomes the road. Only then does the story go on. The women arrive, out of breath, and Krishna greets them like a polite host. Then he tells them to go home. The night is dark, the forest full of animals, your families will be looking for you, your place is with them. It's a test, and it lands hard. The gopis stand with eyes down, scratching the ground with their toes, crying. Then they answer. Their hearts were taken by him, they say, and their feet won't carry them back. They came not for a household but for him. Krishna smiles, stays, and the night of play in the forest begins. As he honors them, the women grow proud, each one sure she is the most favored woman in the world. At that moment, the text says, Krishna vanishes. Some devotional teachers read the whole episode as the soul's longing for God, told in the language of human love; Parikshit's question is the text's own reminder to read it that way.
screen: `ANY FEELING, TURNED TO HIM.` · `GO HOME, HE SAYS.` · `OUR FEET WON'T CARRY US BACK.` · then, large: `PRIDE, AND HE VANISHES.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle and watch where your mind points on its own: a person, a worry, a plan. Each time you catch it, name the direction quietly, toward work, toward someone, toward tomorrow, and come back to the breath. If you pray, turn your mind toward God, or toward Krishna, for one breath, then simply watch again.

segments.voice: Have you seen him? The gopis are asking the trees. They go from one to the next in the moonlit forest, a fig, a tulsi plant, a jasmine vine, asking whether he passed this way. Nobody answers. A moment ago they were sure they were the luckiest women alive. Now they're searching the forest floor for a footprint.
screen: `HAVE YOU SEEN HIM?` → `ASKING THE TREES.` → `THE SEARCH, THE SONG, THE CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: They do find footprints, his, and beside them a woman's. He has taken one gopi with him. But she grows proud too, asks him to carry her, and he vanishes from her as well. The others find her weeping alone, and now they're all in the same place: together, without him. So they go down to the bank of the Yamuna and sing. Tradition calls their song the Gopi Gita. It has a reproach or two, but mostly it's a long remembering, his walk, his flute, his face coming home with the cows at dusk, and running through it, the plain plea to show himself. Then he's there, smiling, a garland around his neck. He tells them he stepped away so their love would deepen, the way a poor man who finds treasure and loses it thinks of nothing else. Then the one they worship says something startling: he can't repay them. Only then does the dance itself happen, the rasa. The women form a circle, and Krishna appears between every two of them, so each one feels him at her side. Not a share of him. All of him, beside each one. Devotees take this as a picture of how God loves: wholly, each soul as if it were the only one. In Braj, many temples keep the autumn full moon, Sharad Purnima, as the night of this dance. And the Bhagavata closes with one more frame: whoever hears this with faith gains devotion and is freed from the craving that troubles the heart.

902.hook: Kamsa's messenger rides to Vraja full of longing, and rolls in the dust of Krishna's footprints

902.howItsDone: Akrura is remembered by devotees as a model of vandanam, bowing in prayer; pilgrims to Vrindavan touch the dust of Braj to their foreheads, some circle Govardhan bowing full length, and the chapters of Akrura's journey are recited at katha.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rasa lila ended in the circle on the moonlit night, with Krishna wholly beside every one of the gopis.
screen: `RASA LILA.` · `KRISHNA BESIDE EACH ONE.`

segments.voice: A chariot is on the road to Vraja, and its driver is carrying a trap. King Kamsa of Mathura has learned that the cowherd boy everyone talks about is the son he was warned of, the one born to kill him. So Kamsa plans a festival: a contest of wrestlers, and an elephant at the gate. All he needs is someone the boys will trust to bring them. He chooses Akrura, a respected elder of their own clan. Akrura agrees to go.
screen: `A CHARIOT CARRYING A TRAP.` → `KAMSA NEEDS A MESSENGER.` → `AKRURA AGREES TO GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the surprise. Akrura is Kamsa's messenger, and Krishna's devotee. The Bhagavata spends the whole ride inside his head, and what's there isn't dread. It's longing. All the way he turns one thought over: I'm going to see him. Will Krishna look at him kindly, or hold him at arm's length as the king's man? He reaches Vraja at sunset, as the cows come home. In the dust of the cow pen he sees footprints, and knows whose they are; the text says they carry the marks devotees look for on the soles of Krishna's feet. Akrura jumps down from his chariot and rolls in that dust, overcome. Then Krishna and Balarama come out to meet him. No arm's length. The brothers embrace him, take his hand, lead him in, wash his feet and feed him. Krishna asks after his family, and only then asks what brought him. And Akrura, the king's messenger, tells them everything: Kamsa's hatred, the festival, the plan. Krishna and Balarama laugh, and agree to go. Akrura's bow in the dust is a moment devotees treasure. A well-known verse in the Krishna tradition names one great devotee for each of bhakti's nine ways, and Akrura is its model of vandanam, bowing in prayer. And the dust became holy too. Pilgrims to Vrindavan still touch the dust of Braj to their foreheads, and some go around Govardhan bowing full length on the ground, because Krishna walked there. The road was the king's errand. The bow was Akrura's own.
screen: `THE KING'S MAN, AND KRISHNA'S DEVOTEE.` · `FOOTPRINTS IN THE DUST.` · `WASHED, FED, ASKED AFTER.` · then, large: `VANDANAM: BOWING IN THE DUST.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus begin the day by touching the floor and then their forehead, and bow at the feet of elders the same way: a small vandanam. Try it now. Touch the ground, bring your hand to your forehead, and think of a place where God has felt near to you. If you pray, bow there in your mind, the way Akrura bowed in the dust of Vraja. If you don't, touch the floor and thank one place, or one person, that has held something good for you.

segments.voice: The news gets around the village overnight. By morning everyone knows: Akrura has come from Mathura, and he's taking Krishna and Balarama with him. The cowherd men load carts with pots of milk and butter as gifts for the king. And the gopis, who ran into the forest at the sound of a flute, stand in the road beside the chariot. This time there's nothing to run toward.
screen: `THE NEWS GETS AROUND OVERNIGHT.` → `CARTS LOADED FOR MATHURA.` → `THE ONES WHO STAY.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata gives the gopis a long, raw lament, and doesn't tidy it up. They blame the creator, who brings people together and pulls them apart for no reason, like a child playing and spoiling the game. They turn on Akrura too. His name means not cruel, they say, and it doesn't fit: he's come to carry off the one thing they have. They imagine the women of Mathura, who will see Krishna every day now, and wonder whether a city boy will remember village girls. Then they stop caring what anyone thinks, and cry out his names in the road. The chariot moves. Krishna sees them and sends back word through a messenger, as the text puts it: I will come back. And the gopis stand watching until the flag on the chariot and the dust behind it are gone. Look at the shape of this week: hearing him, emptying out for him, running to him as they were, finding him beside every one. Now the same love has nowhere to go, and it doesn't stop. Hindu devotion has a name for this: viraha, love in separation. Many teachers, especially in the Krishna traditions of Braj and Bengal, hold that longing for God while apart isn't a failure of love but one of its deepest forms, because the mind never leaves him. Poets like Surdas filled songbooks with the gopis' longing. The story will come back to these women.
screen: `THEY BLAME THE CREATOR, AND AKRURA.` · `I WILL COME BACK.` · `UNTIL THE DUST IS GONE.` · then, large: `VIRAHA: LOVE THAT LONGS.`

segments.voice: Songs of viraha are sung wherever Krishna is loved. Bring to mind someone who is far from you, on a trip, in a new city, or further, and let yourself be one of the ones standing in the road; if there's an ache, don't push it away. If you pray, let the ache become a call, and say Krishna's name, or God's, softly, the way the gopis called his names. If you don't, hold that person in mind with thanks, without asking for anything.
